title: Interest rates and bond prices
subtitle: Bond pricing basics
openingQuestion: You're holding a bond with a fixed 6%/year coupon. Market interest rates on newly issued bonds suddenly rise to 8%/year. What happens to your 6% bond's price on the secondary market?
openingOptions: It falls, because the new 8% bonds are more attractive
Your bond will automatically mature early the moment market rates rise
The bond's price won't change at all, because the coupon rate was fixed at issuance
The price will rise, because a bond issued earlier is always worth more than a newly issued one
explanation: When market rates rise, an older bond with a lower coupon becomes less attractive relative to a new one. To still be sold, the older bond's holder has to accept a price below face value, so the actual yield a new buyer earns matches the market's 8%. This is the inverse relationship between interest rates and bond prices.

diagram.label: The old bond still pays a fixed 6% coupon
To sell, its price must drop below face value
The new buyer thereby still earns an 8% yield

realWorldExample.company: US Government bonds as the Fed raised rates in 2022-2023
realWorldExample.description: During 2022-2023, the US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate repeatedly to fight inflation. 10-year US government bonds issued earlier with a low coupon (around 1.5-2%) fell sharply in price on the secondary market, at times losing 15-20% of their value, because investors could buy new bonds at a much higher rate (up to 4-5%). Several US banks, including Silicon Valley Bank, held large amounts of these low-coupon, long-term bonds and recorded huge unrealized losses as prices fell - one of the causes behind that bank's collapse in 2023.

quiz.question: Market interest rates fall from 6% to 4%. What happens to the price of an outstanding bond with a fixed 6% coupon?
options: The bond's price doesn't change at all from when it was issued
The bond's price falls below the original price it was issued at
The bond gets cancelled and the issuer must immediately return all the principal to the investor
The price rises, because a 6% coupon is now more attractive than the current 4% rate
quiz.explanation: When market rates fall, an older bond with the higher coupon (6%) becomes relatively more attractive than a new bond (only 4%). Investors are willing to pay above face value to own that higher interest stream, pushing the bond's price up.

quiz.question: Why is the relationship between market interest rates and bond prices always inverse?
options: Because the coupon is fixed, so the price must adjust for the yield to match, and this rule holds no matter which currency the bond happens to be denominated in
Because a bond's price only depends on its remaining term
Because it's an administrative rule set by the State Bank
Because interest rates and bond prices have no direct link at all
quiz.explanation: Since a fixed coupon cannot change after issuance, the only way for a bond's actual yield to reflect the new interest-rate level is by adjusting its trading price on the secondary market - the price falls when rates rise, and rises when rates fall.

quiz.question: A bond has a 100-million face value and a 6% coupon. Market rates rise to 8%. What happens to this bond's price now?
options: Below 100 million, so the yield a new buyer earns reaches 8%
Still exactly 100 million, because face value is fixed, something easy to get backwards at first
Above 100 million, because higher rates make every bond more valuable
Can't be determined without knowing whether the issuer is the Government or a company
quiz.explanation: No one will pay 100 million for a bond paying 6 million/year when 100 million elsewhere buys 8 million/year. The only way the old bond can sell is by lowering its price, so the 6 million in interest plus the price discount to maturity together equal an 8% yield.

quiz.question: You're holding a bond to maturity. How does the bond's price rising and falling in the meantime affect you?
options: Partly, because the coupon is adjusted each period based on the bond's price
Directly, because the principal returned is calculated based on the market price
Not at all - you still receive the full coupon and face value at maturity
Not at all, because the issuer compensates for the price difference, a factor that changes the calculation meaningfully
quiz.explanation: Price swings only become real if you sell. Holding to maturity locks in your cash flow from the day you bought: regular coupons plus face value at the end. This is why an investor buying bonds for steady income cares little about the day-to-day price.

quiz.question: Why do long-term bonds swing in price more sharply than short-term bonds when rates change?
options: Because long-term bonds are usually issued by higher-risk companies, even though this company operates in an industry regulators consider unusually low-risk
Because long-term bonds have a higher coupon, so the price gap is also larger
Because long-term bonds have lower liquidity, so their price is easier to push around
Because there are more future coupon periods, farther out, that must be discounted at the new rate
quiz.explanation: A bond's price is the sum of its future cash flows, discounted. A 20-year bond has 20 coupon periods plus a principal payment far in the future, all affected by the new discount rate; a 1-year bond has almost just one period. This sensitivity is measured by duration.

quiz.question: If you expect interest rates to fall sharply soon, which bond strategy fits?
options: Buy long-term bonds, since the price rise will be larger when rates fall
Sell all your bonds and move entirely into short-term savings deposits
Only buy bonds with a term under three months
Stop buying bonds altogether, since falling rates always drag bond prices down with them
quiz.explanation: The inverse relationship runs both ways: when rates fall, bond prices rise, and rise the most at long terms. But this is a bet on the direction of rates - if the guess is wrong, that same long term is exactly what makes the loss the heaviest.

keyTakeaways: Bond prices and market interest rates always move in opposite directions: rates up means bond prices down, and vice versa
The reason: the coupon on an already-issued bond never changes, so the price must adjust for the actual yield to match the new interest-rate level
If you hold a bond to maturity, price swings in between don't affect the principal and interest you receive - they only matter if you want to sell early

practicePrompt.question: You're holding a corporate bond with a 7%/year coupon, 4 years left to maturity. Market rates have just fallen from 7% to 5%. If you want to sell this bond right now on the secondary market, what is the selling price likely to look like?
options: Above the original face value, because the fixed 7% coupon is now more attractive than the current 5% rate, so new buyers are willing to pay more to own this bond
Below the original face value, because falling market rates always devalue every outstanding bond, even when market interest rates have not moved from where they stood at issuance
Exactly the same as the original face value, because secondary-market bond prices aren't affected by interest rates
Impossible to determine, because secondary-market bond prices don't follow any predictable pattern
practicePrompt.explanation: When market rates fall, a bond with a higher fixed coupon becomes more attractive, pushing its price up on the secondary market.

summary.keyIdea: Bond prices and market interest rates always move in opposite directions: rates up means bond prices down, and vice versa
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a line to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Try simulating a price swing
application.message: Suppose you hold an 8%-coupon bond. Work out for yourself what happens to its price if market rates rise to 10% - would you have to sell below or above face value?
application.secondary: Reasoning through it once yourself sticks far better than memorizing the inverse rule.

sections.text: This is one of the most important rules of the bond market, and also what confuses many newcomers: when interest rates rise, bond prices fall, and when interest rates fall, bond prices rise.
Why does this inverse relationship exist?

Imagine you're holding a bond with a 100-million-dong face value and a fixed 6%/year coupon, bought last year. This year, market rates rise and newly issued bonds pay an 8%/year coupon. If you want to sell your 6% bond to someone else, they'll compare: why buy a bond paying only 6% when a new one pays 8%? To convince a buyer, you have to lower your selling price below 100 million dong, so that the 6% interest plus the discount from buying below face value together match the market's 8% yield.

sections.label: A simplified example
sections.text: A bond with a 100-million face value, a 6%/year coupon (6 million dong/year), and 1 year left to maturity. If market rates rise to 8%, for a new buyer to earn an equivalent 8% yield, this bond's market price will have to fall to about 98.1 million dong instead of 100 million - because then (6 million interest + 1.9 million price discount) / 98.1 million ≈ 8%.
What does this mean for an ordinary bond buyer?

items: If you buy a bond and hold it to maturity, price swings in between don't matter - you still receive the full periodic interest and the full face value at maturity
Price swings only really matter if you need to sell before maturity, or if you invest through a bond fund - where net asset value (NAV) moves with the market price of the bonds inside the fund
The longer a bond's term, the more sensitive its price is to interest-rate swings - covered in more detail in a separate lesson on interest rate risk

left.label: Market rates rise
left.text: An older bond (with the lower coupon) becomes relatively less attractive → its price falls on the secondary market.

right.label: Market rates fall
right.text: An older bond (with the higher coupon) becomes relatively more attractive → its price rises on the secondary market.

sections.text: Understanding this rule keeps you from panicking when you see the value of a bond fund you hold fall during a period when the State Bank or the Fed is raising rates - that's normal market movement, not a sign the bonds are 'bad' or the issuer is about to default.

lines: Bond prices and market interest rates always move in opposite directions - this is the rule, not the exception.
If you hold a bond to maturity, temporary price swings don't change the final amount you receive.
